items.definition: An overview of how different power plant types convert an energy source into electricity, mostly by spinning a generator with steam or directly with a moving force.
items.core_idea: Most generation (fossil, nuclear, geothermal) works by using heat to make steam that spins an electromagnet-based generator; wind, hydro, and solar are the main exceptions that either spin the generator directly (wind, hydro) or skip rotation entirely (solar).
key_points: Fossil fuel plants (oil, gas, coal) burn fuel to create steam that spins a generator; all fossil fuels emit CO2 when burned.
Coal generation produces roughly 2-3x the pollution of the other fossil fuels.

Nuclear plants use fission to boil water into steam; a pound of highly enriched uranium is roughly equivalent to a million gallons of gasoline in energy content, but enriched uranium faces supply shortages and disposal/storage difficulty.
Geothermal plants use naturally occurring underground steam and are efficient but geographically limited to specific locations.
Wind turbines spin generator windings directly using wind force rather than steam.
Hydroelectric dams spin generators using falling or flowing water.
Solar facilities convert sunlight directly to electricity without a spinning generator.
relationships: Fuel choice drives emissions profile and plant economics discussed later in heat rate and dispatch order concepts.
trading_implications: Generation mix (coal vs. gas vs. renewables) underlies supply-side fundamentals that drive locational and time-of-day price behavior.
common_misunderstandings: Not all power plants use steam turbines — wind, hydro, and solar bypass the heat-to-steam process entirely.

items.definition: Cogeneration is the practice of capturing and selling the steam byproduct of electricity generation instead of venting it, so a plant produces both power and usable heat.
items.core_idea: Reusing waste steam as a saleable product lowers a plant's effective operating cost, and the order in which heat vs. electricity is produced defines whether it is a topping or bottoming cycle plant.
key_points: Cogeneration plants sell both electricity and steam/heat, which reduces net operating cost versus a plant that only sells power.
Topping cycle plants generate electricity first, then use the leftover exhaust steam for heating.
Bottoming cycle plants generate heat first for an industrial process, then use the leftover heat to run a steam generator for electricity.
relationships: Related to heat rate, since cogeneration changes a plant's effective economics even if fuel-to-electricity efficiency is unchanged.
trading_implications: Cogeneration economics can make a plant willing to run at lower power prices than a pure generation asset because of the added steam revenue stream.
common_misunderstandings: Cogeneration plants are not purely electricity assets — their dispatch economics depend on steam/heat sales too, so evaluating them on power price alone is incomplete.

items.definition: Heat rate measures how efficiently a power plant converts fuel into electricity, expressed as fuel energy input needed per unit of electrical output.
items.core_idea: A lower heat rate means a plant needs less fuel input to produce the same electrical output, i.e., it is more efficient.
key_points: Heat rate is expressed as a ratio of heat (fuel) input to electrical work output.
Common units are Btu/kWh or MMBtu/MWh.
Lower heat rate = more efficient plant.

formulas.name: Heat rate
formulas.formula: Heat rate = Fuel energy input / Electrical energy output

variables.Fuel energy input: Btu or MMBtu of fuel burned
variables.Electrical energy output: kWh or MWh of electricity produced

relationships: Heat rate is a core input to plant dispatch cost and is later used to convert fuel prices into an implied power price (spark spread type logic).
trading_implications: Plant heat rate determines fuel cost per MWh generated, which underlies merit-order dispatch and marginal price setting in the grid.
common_misunderstandings: A 'lower' heat rate is better (more efficient), which can be counterintuitive since lower numbers usually connote worse performance in other contexts.

items.topic: Transmission vs. distribution and the power grid
items.definition: Transmission is the bulk, long-distance movement of power at high voltage from a power plant to a substation; distribution is the shorter, low-voltage movement of power from a substation to end consumers.
items.core_idea: The power grid links generation, transmission lines, and substations into an interconnected network whose redundancy — multiple routing paths between any two points — is what prevents a single failed line from causing a blackout.
key_points: Transmission = bulk transfer at high voltage, plant to substation.
Distribution = transfer at lower voltage, substation to consumers.
The grid's redundancy (multiple paths between locations) prevents overload on any single line and protects against single-point-of-failure blackouts.
Most lines are overhead on poles; buried lines are used in some urban areas but are less reliable and harder to maintain, and are uncommon in suburban/rural areas.
Higher voltage reduces transmission losses (power dissipated as heat) but increases danger, so voltage/routing choices trade off safety, reliability, and efficiency.
Transformers step voltage up for long-distance transmission and step it back down for local distribution.
relationships: Transmission losses and congestion connect to locational marginal pricing and FTRs.
trading_implications: Grid topology and line capacity constraints are the physical root cause of congestion pricing and the need for FTR hedges.
common_misunderstandings: Burying power lines, while common in cities for aesthetics/safety, actually reduces reliability and maintainability rather than improving it.

items.definition: AC (alternating current) and DC (direct current) are the two ways electrical energy propagates through a wire: DC moves via the physical drift of electrons, AC moves via an electromagnetic shockwave created by oscillating the field.
items.core_idea: AC dominates modern transmission because its voltage is easy to step up or down, but it requires all generators on a grid to oscillate in precise synchronization, whereas DC avoids synchronization but suffers voltage drop past each load point, making grid-wide voltage hard to predict.
key_points: Both AC and DC are created by placing a conductive wire in an electromagnetic field, pushing electrons from the negative to positive side.
DC power is the direct motion of electrons down the wire.
AC power is an electromagnetic shockwave (created by electron collisions when the field/charge oscillates) that propagates much faster than individual electrons move.
AC's advantage: voltage is easy to scale up or down, simplifying transmission system design.

AC's challenge: every generator on the grid must oscillate in exact synchrony, or shockwaves from different generators collide and cancel out; this synchronization problem grows harder as more generators are added.
DC's issue: voltage declines on the line after each point where power is drawn off, making voltage hard to predict across a grid with variable demand.
DC's advantage: DC generators don't need to synchronize with other power plants.
relationships: Underlies why real-world grids (including ERCOT) are AC systems requiring frequency synchronization.
trading_implications: Not directly a trading mechanic, but explains a physical constraint (synchronization) behind grid reliability events that can drive price volatility.
common_misunderstandings: AC power is not the electrons themselves moving long distances — it's a shockwave/electromagnetic wave propagating through the electrons, which is why it travels far faster than electron drift speed.
related_topics: Transmission vs. distribution and the power grid

items.definition: Locational marginal price (LMP) is the price of power at a specific grid location, which diverges from the grid-wide price when transmission lines connecting cheap generation to demand become overloaded and force out-of-order (more expensive) generators to run.
items.core_idea: With unlimited transmission capacity, power would cost the same everywhere (set by the most recently activated/marginal generator), but when lines congest, only customers in the congested area bear the extra cost of activating pricier, closer-in generation.
key_points: Absent transmission constraints, price is uniform across the grid and equals the cost of the last (marginal) generator dispatched.
During peak demand, lines from low-cost generation to load can become overloaded, forcing more expensive, closer generators online out of normal cost order.
The extra cost from this reordering is charged only to consumers in the congested location, not spread across the whole grid — this location-specific price is the LMP.
Most of the U.S. is moving toward LMP-based cost allocation.
relationships: Congestion and LMP directly motivate the existence of financial transmission rights (FTRs) as a hedging instrument.
trading_implications: Traders/consumers exposed to a node with frequent congestion face basis risk versus the broader hub price, which is the risk FTRs are designed to hedge.
common_misunderstandings: LMP differences are not arbitrary pricing — they specifically reflect the cost of activating out-of-merit-order generation to relieve a physical line overload.
related_topics: Transmission vs. distribution and the power grid

items.topic: Financial transmission rights (FTRs) and FTR options
items.definition: An FTR is a bilateral contract where two parties settle on the difference in price between two grid nodes, letting a power buyer hedge the risk of paying a higher congestion-driven price at their delivery point versus a reference node.
items.core_idea: FTRs let market participants hedge locational basis risk created by congestion; because the payment obligation under a plain FTR can run either direction, FTR options exist to let a buyer pay an upfront premium to cap their downside instead of taking on a two-way obligation.
key_points: FTRs are contracts between two counterparties who take opposite sides of an obligation to pay/receive the price difference between two nodes.
If there is no congestion, the two nodes' prices match and no payment is owed.
If there is congestion, one party pays the other; either party can end up owing depending on how prices diverge.
FTR options let a party pay an upfront premium to avoid the obligation to pay under the FTR later — effectively insurance against adverse congestion pricing.
The purpose of FTRs is to help customers manage price risk from buying power at a major hub node while ultimately paying a congestion-driven price at their actual location.
relationships: Directly tied to congestion and LMP — FTRs exist because of the node-to-node price divergence congestion creates.
trading_implications: FTRs (and FTR options) are the standard hedge for locational basis risk between a hub and a delivery node; an FTR is a swap-like symmetric obligation while an FTR option is a capped-downside, premium-paid hedge.
common_misunderstandings: A plain FTR is not one-directional insurance — either party can end up paying, unlike an FTR option where the premium payer's downside is capped.
